title: Realised volatility
objectives: Compute realised volatility over different windows.
Annualise it correctly and choose a window by trading noise against delay.

screens.prose: "How volatile is share B?" Four analysts answer on day 1,999. Each takes the sd of B's daily returns over a different number of recent days and scales it to a year.
screens.question: Who is right?

options.text: All four: each answers a different question about a different stretch of days.
Dee: more days always give the right answer.
options.why: You assumed the longest window wins. Volatility moves, so 250 days mixes a whole year of weather into one number.

options.text: Ana: the most recent days matter most.
options.why: You trusted 5 days. Five returns give an sd that is off by about a third either way.

options.text: None: they should all agree.
options.why: They would agree only if volatility were constant. Lesson 1 showed it is not.

hints.text: Would the four numbers agree if volatility never changed?
With clustering, different stretches really do have different volatility.
Each figure is an honest estimate for its own window. The skill is choosing the window for the job.

feedback.correct: That's it. A volatility figure is incomplete without its window.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what each window measures, given that volatility moves.

explain.text: 11.44%, 15.11%, 12.18% and 13.90% are all correct calculations. They differ because volatility moves and because short windows are noisy. This lesson is about choosing between them.

screens.prose: **Rolling volatility** of B over days 1,200 to 1,699, through the storm. The dashed line is the true volatility, which we know because we simulated B. Slide through the four windows.

options.text: 5 days
options.why: You picked the fastest. It reacts at once but jumps about: it swings far above and below the dashed line.

options.text: 20 days
60 days

options.why: You picked the smoothest. It barely notices the storm and is highest after it ends.

hints.text: Look for a line that is neither jumpy nor late.

feedback.correct: Correct. Short windows are noisy and fast; long ones smooth and slow. 20 days balances the two here.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare each window's noise and its delay against the dashed line.

explain.text: A 5-day window reacts at once but is noisy; a 250-day window is smooth but months late. In between, 20 days follows the storm closely for B. We will measure that trade-off exactly.

screens.title: Realised volatility
screens.prose: The sd of recent returns is **realised volatility**. Over the last 20 days, B's daily sd is 0.9516%. Volatility is quoted a year. With 252 trading days and uncorrelated daily returns, variances add, so the annual variance is 252 times the daily (from `estimation` lesson 8).
screens.question: What is the annualised 20-day realised volatility?

hints.text: If the variance scales by 252, how does the sd scale?
Take the square root of 252.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The variance scales by 252, so the sd scales by $\sqrt{252}$.

byKey.365: You used 365 calendar days. Returns come only on trading days, about 252 a year.
byKey.times252: You multiplied the sd by 252. That scaling is for the variance; the sd takes $\sqrt{252}$.
byKey.daily: That is the daily figure. Scale it to a year.

explain.text: Annual variance is $252\sigma^2$, so annual volatility is $\sqrt{252}\,\sigma = 15.87 \times 0.9516\% = 15.11\%$. This is how every figure in this course is annualised. It needs the daily returns to be uncorrelated, which `arma` and lesson 2 confirmed for B.

screens.prose: Desks often skip the mean and use $\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum r_t^2}$: the zero-mean realised volatility. For daily returns the mean is tiny next to the sd. The table compares both on B's last days.
screens.question: Why do the two disagree so much at 5 days?

options.text: B fell about 0.89% a day for those 5 days; the sample sd subtracts that run as if it were a known mean.
The sample sd divides by 4 and the other by 5.
options.why: That changes the result by a factor of $\sqrt{5/4}$, about 12%. The gap here is 52%.

options.text: One of the two formulas is wrong.
options.why: Both are standard. They disagree only when the window's mean is large next to its sd.

options.text: Zero-mean volatility is always higher.
options.why: At 60 and 250 days the two differ by less than 0.1 points.

hints.text: When is the sample mean of a window far from 0?
Over the last 5 days B's returns average about −0.89% a day.
Subtracting a 5-day mean of −0.89% removes most of the movement. Over long windows the mean is close to 0 and the two agree.

feedback.correct: Correct. Over 5 days the mean is noise, and subtracting it throws real movement away.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the window's mean with its sd.

explain.text: A daily mean of −0.89% is larger than the spread left around it, so the sample sd shrinks to 11.44% while the zero-mean figure is 17.43%. Over 60 or 250 days the mean is near 0 and the two match. Desks use the zero-mean version because a short window's mean is mostly noise.

screens.prose: How far off can a window be? For normal returns with constant $\sigma$, the standard error of $\hat\sigma$ from $n$ days is about $\sigma/\sqrt{2n}$ (`estimation` lesson 8). As a share of $\sigma$ it is $1/\sqrt{2n}$.
screens.question: Fill in $1/\sqrt{2n}$ for each window, as a percentage of $\sigma$.

hints.text: 31.6%, 15.8% and 4.5%: quadrupling $n$ halves the error.

feedback.correct: Correct. A 5-day figure of 15% could easily be 10% or 20%; a 250-day figure is good to about ±0.7 points.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $1/\sqrt{2n}$ and enter it as a percentage.

explain.text: Five days give $\pm 31.6\%$ of $\sigma$, 20 days $\pm 15.8\%$, 250 days $\pm 4.5\%$. Long windows are precise about a stretch of the past in which $\sigma$ itself moved. That is the trade-off you saw on the chart: noise against delay.

screens.prose: Write the analysts' calculation. `annualise` scales any per-period sd to a year: $\sqrt{252}$ for days, $\sqrt{52}$ for weeks. On B's last 5, 20, 60 and 250 days you should get 0.1144, 0.1511, 0.1218 and 0.1390.
screens.question: Complete `annualise(sd, periods_per_year)` and `realised_vol(r, window, annualise_it=True, zero_mean=False)` on the last `window` days.

widget.prelude:
import numpy as np

def simulate_garch(omega, alpha, beta, n, seed):
    """GARCH(1,1) returns: r_t = sigma_t z_t, z_t ~ N(0, 1),
    sigma2_t = omega + alpha r_{t-1}^2 + beta sigma2_{t-1}, started at the long-run variance."""
    z = np.random.default_rng(seed).standard_normal(n)
    r = np.empty(n); s2 = np.empty(n)
    s2[0] = omega / (1 - alpha - beta)
    for t in range(n):
        if t > 0:
            s2[t] = omega + alpha * r[t - 1] ** 2 + beta * s2[t - 1]
        r[t] = np.sqrt(s2[t]) * z[t]
    return r, s2

# The course data set: 2,000 days of a simulated share's daily returns (decimals).
r, s2 = simulate_garch(2e-6, 0.08, 0.90, 2000, 7)
# The contrast: independent normal returns with sd 1%.
iid = 0.01 * np.random.default_rng(8).standard_normal(2000)
widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests: `r` at 5, 20, 60 and 250 days rounded to 4 places, 20 days to 6 places with each option, `annualise` for daily and weekly data, and a 4-day list. `r` is loaded. The first run loads NumPy, which takes a few seconds.

`np.std(x, ddof=1)` and `np.sqrt(np.mean(x ** 2))` are the two sds.
`return sd * np.sqrt(periods_per_year)`; `sd = np.sqrt(np.mean(x ** 2))` and `sd = np.std(x, ddof=1)`.

feedback.correct: Correct. Your four figures match the analysts'.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Scale by the square root of the periods, and use ddof 1 only for the sample sd.

explain.text: `[-window:]` takes the last `window` returns, so the estimate is for the days just gone. The zero-mean version does not subtract the mean, so it divides by $n$. `annualise(0.02, 52)` turns a 2% weekly sd into 14.42% a year.

screens.prose: Measure the trade-off. Each evening, estimate tomorrow's variance by the rolling variance of the last $w$ days, and compare it with the true $\sigma_t^2$ from the simulation. The chart shows the root mean squared error over days 250 to 1,999.
screens.question: Tap the window with the smallest error.

hints.text: Find the lowest point.
The curve falls steeply from 5 days, then rises slowly.
The minimum among these is at 20 days, with error 0.435.

feedback.correct: Correct. Among these windows, 20 days has the least error for B.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap the lowest point on the chart.

byKey.w250: You picked the longest window. It is precise about the past year but slow, and its error is the largest here.
byKey.w5: You picked the fastest window. Its noise makes its error more than twice the minimum.
byKey.w15: Close, but 15 days is a little noisier than 20.
byKey.w30: Close, but 30 days is a little slower than 20.

explain.text: Short windows lose to noise, long ones to delay; for B the balance is near 20 days (22 over every window from 5 to 250). The best window depends on how fast volatility moves, so it differs from share to share. Level 2's EWMA and GARCH avoid choosing a hard cut-off at all.

screens.prose: Now find the best window in code. `s2` holds B's true daily variances. The estimate for day $t$ is the sample variance of days $t - w$ to $t - 1$: known the evening before. Score every window on the same days, from day `max(windows)` on.
screens.question: Complete `best_window(r, true_var, windows)`: the window with the least mean squared error against `true_var`.

import numpy as np

def simulate_garch(omega, alpha, beta, n, seed):
    """GARCH(1,1) returns: r_t = sigma_t z_t, z_t ~ N(0, 1),
    sigma2_t = omega + alpha r_{t-1}^2 + beta sigma2_{t-1}, started at the long-run variance."""
    z = np.random.default_rng(seed).standard_normal(n)
    r = np.empty(n); s2 = np.empty(n)
    s2[0] = omega / (1 - alpha - beta)
    for t in range(n):
        if t > 0:
            s2[t] = omega + alpha * r[t - 1] ** 2 + beta * s2[t - 1]
        r[t] = np.sqrt(s2[t]) * z[t]
    return r, s2

# The course data set: 2,000 days of a simulated share's daily returns (decimals).
r, s2 = simulate_garch(2e-6, 0.08, 0.90, 2000, 7)
# The contrast: independent normal returns with sd 1%.
iid = 0.01 * np.random.default_rng(8).standard_normal(2000)
widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests on `r` with its true variances `s2`, on `iid` with its constant true variance 0.0001, and on the first 600 days. Each estimate must use only days up to yesterday; a window that includes today scores differently. The first run loads NumPy and pandas, which takes a few seconds; the 246-window test takes about a second.

hints.text: `rolling(w).var()` ends each window today; you need it to end yesterday.
`.shift(1)` moves every estimate one day later, so day $t$ gets the window ending on day $t - 1$.
`est = pd.Series(r, dtype=float).rolling(w).var().shift(1).to_numpy()` and `errors[w] = np.mean((est[start:] - true_var[start:]) ** 2)`.

feedback.correct: Correct. 20 days wins among the nine, 22 over every window, and 250 for the independent series.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Shift the rolling variance by one day, and score every window from the same first day.

explain.text: For the independent series the true variance never moves, so delay costs nothing and the longest window wins. For B, volatility moves, so a shorter window wins. The `shift(1)` matters: an estimate that includes today's return peeks at the answer.

screens.prose: A share's daily returns have an sd of 1%, so a daily variance of 0.0001. Three colleagues annualise it and get three different answers. One answer is right.
screens.question: What is the annual volatility?

options.why: You scaled by $\sqrt{365}$. Returns arrive on trading days only, about 252 a year.
You multiplied the variance by $\sqrt{252}$ and took the root: $\sqrt{0.0001 \times 15.87} = 3.98\%$. Variance scales by 252 itself.
You multiplied the sd by 252. Only the variance scales by 252; the sd scales by $\sqrt{252}$.

hints.text: Which scales by 252, the variance or the sd?
Annual variance $= 252 \times 0.0001 = 0.0252$.

feedback.correct: That's it. Variance scales by the number of periods; the sd by its square root.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Scale the variance by 252 trading days, then take the root.

byKey.365: You used calendar days. With 252 trading days, $\sqrt{252} \times 1\% = 15.87\%$.
byKey.var: You applied $\sqrt{252}$ to the variance. The variance takes 252; the root comes after.

explain.text: Annual variance is $252 \times 0.0001 = 0.0252$, so annual volatility is $\sqrt{0.0252} = 15.87\%$. The same rule turns weekly data into a year with $\sqrt{52}$ and daily into weekly with $\sqrt{5}$. A 252 applied to weekly data, or a 365 applied to trading days, overstates the risk.

screens.prose: Edge case. Take the independent series A and make day 1,000 a crash of −10%. The chart shows its 20-day volatility from day 950 to day 1,059. Day 1,000 enters the window at once.
screens.question: On which day does the 20-day volatility fall back?

widget.label: Day it falls back
widget.accept: Day 1,020: the 20-day windows ending on days 1,000 to 1,019 hold the crash.

hints.text: Which windows contain day 1,000?
A 20-day window ending on day $t$ holds days $t - 19$ to $t$.
The last window holding day 1,000 ends on day 1,019. Day 1,020's window is clear.

feedback.correct: Correct. The crash props the figure up for exactly 20 days, then drops out at once.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the 20 windows that hold day 1,000.

byKey.off-by-one: Day 1,019's window still holds days 1,000 to 1,019, crash included.
byKey.next: Day 1,020's window, days 1,001 to 1,020, is already clear.
byKey.now: The figure stays high while day 1,000 is in the window.

explain.text: The 20-day figure jumps from 16.7% to 38.4% on day 1,000, stays there for 20 days, then falls to 12.4% on day 1,020, though nothing happened that day. That cliff is the **ghost** of the crash, an artefact of equal weights. Level 2's exponentially weighted average lets old days fade instead of dropping off.

screens.prose: You have used $\sqrt{252}$ all lesson. Derive it. A year's log return is the sum of 252 daily log returns $r_1, \dots, r_{252}$, each with variance $\sigma^2$.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $r_{\text{year}} = r_1 + r_2 + \dots + r_{252}$, since log returns add over days
$\text{Var}(r_{\text{year}}) = \sum_i \text{Var}(r_i) + \sum_{i \ne j} \text{Cov}(r_i, r_j)$, the variance of a sum
$= 252\,\sigma^2$, since uncorrelated days have zero covariance and each variance is $\sigma^2$

hints.text: Start from what a year's return is made of.
The variance of a sum has variance terms and covariance terms.
Sum, then the variance of the sum, then drop the covariances, then the root.

feedback.correct: Correct. The rule needs uncorrelated returns, not independent ones, which is why it survives clustering.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Build the year's return first, then its variance, then the root.

byKey.root: The root comes last: it turns the variance you derived into an sd.
byKey.zero: You can only drop the covariances after writing them down.

explain.text: Every line uses one fact: returns add, a sum's variance includes covariances, uncorrelated days have none, and the sd is the root. Clustering makes returns dependent but not correlated, so $\sqrt{252}$ still holds for the average variance. If daily returns were positively correlated, $\sqrt{252}$ would understate the annual risk.

screens.prose: An options trader looks at the one-year call from `trees` lesson 11: $S = K = 100$, $r = 5\%$. It trades at £12.00, which implies a volatility of 24.1%. The share's realised volatility is 16%. Over the option's life she will hedge it daily.
screens.question: What is the most sensible reading of the gap?

options.text: Options usually price more volatility than is later realised; selling and hedging tends to earn the gap, at the cost of losing in a storm.
The option is mispriced by the gap, so selling it and hedging daily locks in a free profit.
options.why: You treated the gap as an arbitrage. Realised volatility can jump to 40% in a storm, as B's did, and the seller then loses.

options.text: Implied and realised volatility measure the same thing, so they must agree and one figure is wrong.
options.why: They measure different things: the past, against the market's price for the future, which carries a premium.

options.text: Buy the option: 24.1% is the market's best forecast of the share's true volatility.
options.why: You read the implied figure as a forecast. It is a price, and it includes a premium for storm risk.

hints.text: Which figure looks back, and which is a price for the future?
Realised volatility is measured from past returns; implied comes from the option's price.
Implied usually sits above realised: the variance risk premium, paid by buyers for protection against storms.

feedback.correct: Correct. The gap is the variance risk premium: usually positive, and paid for storm risk.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Separate a measurement of the past from a price for the future.

explain.text: Implied volatility is a price for future risk, and buyers of options pay up for protection: the **variance risk premium**. A seller who hedges daily earns roughly the gap between implied and realised variance. Clustering is the risk: a 20-day realised figure of 49% would turn that profit into a loss.

ideas: Realised volatility is the sd of recent returns; every figure needs its window. B's last 5, 20, 60 and 250 days give 11.4%, 15.1%, 12.2% and 13.9%.
Annualise the sd by $\sqrt{252}$, because variances of uncorrelated days add: not 252, not $\sqrt{365}$.
Short windows are noisy (standard error $\sigma/\sqrt{2n}$), long ones late; for B, 20 to 22 days has the least error, and every equal-weight window leaves a ghost.

formula.name: Realised volatility
formula.note: The zero-mean version uses $\frac1n\sum r_i^2$; the two agree except over a few days.

summary.trap: Variance scales with time and the sd with its square root: daily 1% is 15.87% a year, not 252% and not 19.10%.

quiz.prose: A fund reports the sd of its weekly returns as 2%.
quiz.question: What is its annual volatility, in %, to 2 places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. There are 52 weeks a year; scale the sd by $\sqrt{52}$.

byKey.252: You used the daily factor on weekly data. A year has 52 weeks.
byKey.52: You multiplied the sd by 52. Only the variance scales by 52.

quiz.prose: A fund's risk limit is 10% annual volatility.
quiz.question: What daily sd does that allow, in %, to 3 places?

feedback.correct: Correct. Level 3 sizes positions to hit exactly this kind of target.

byKey.252: You divided by 252. The sd scales by $\sqrt{252}$.
byKey.365: You used calendar days. Use 252 trading days.

quiz.prose: A 60-day realised volatility reads 20% a year, and returns are close to normal with steady volatility.
quiz.question: Roughly what is its standard error, in percentage points?

byKey.sqrtn: You used $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$, the standard error of a mean. For an sd it is $\sigma/\sqrt{2n}$.
byKey.share: That is the error as a share of $\sigma$, 9.13%. In points it is 9.13% of 20%.

quiz.prose: A share falls 12% on day 500 and is calm before and after. Its 60-day realised volatility is plotted each day.
quiz.question: When does the plot drop sharply?

options.text: On day 560, when the crash leaves the window.
On day 559.
options.why: Day 559's window, days 500 to 559, still holds the crash.

options.text: It fades smoothly from day 500.
options.why: Equal weights do not fade: the crash counts fully until it leaves.

options.text: It never drops; the crash is in the history.
options.why: A rolling window forgets everything older than 60 days.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A 60-day window ending on day $t$ holds days $t - 59$ to $t$.

explain.text: Windows ending on days 500 to 559 contain the crash. On day 560 the window starts at day 501, and the figure falls off a cliff.
